title: Proof and systems of linear equations
summary: Prove results by induction and by contradiction, disprove them by counterexample, and solve systems of up to three linear equations.

keyterms.definition: Proving P(n) for all n ≥ n₀ by showing P(n₀) is true and that P(k) true implies P(k + 1) true.
The first value (usually n = 1) for which a statement is checked in an induction proof.
Showing that if the statement is true for n = k, then it is true for n = k + 1.
Assume the statement is false and deduce something impossible, so the statement must be true.
A single example for which a general statement fails, which disproves it.
Several linear equations in the same unknowns, to be satisfied simultaneously.
Exactly one set of values satisfies every equation; three planes meet at a single point.
The equations are dependent; the solution set is a line or plane written with a parameter.
A system with no solution, revealed by a row such as 0 = k with k ≠ 0.
A free variable such as λ used to describe infinitely many solutions.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a proof by induction in order.
items: Show the statement is true for n = 1
Assume it is true for n = k
Use the assumption to show it is true for n = k + 1
Conclude it is true for all n ∈ ℤ⁺
questions.explanation: All four parts, including the final conclusion sentence, earn marks.

questions.prompt: To disprove “n² + n + 41 is prime for every positive integer n”, you need…
options: to check every n up to 100
questions.explanation: n = 40 gives 1681 = 41², which is not prime. One failure disproves a universal claim.

questions.statement: A proof by contradiction starts by assuming the statement is false.
questions.explanation: You then derive an impossibility, so the assumption must be wrong.

questions.text: The irrationality of √2 is classically proved by ___.
questions.explanation: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms; then p and q are both even, a contradiction.

questions.prompt: Proving ∑ᵣ₌₁ⁿ r = n(n + 1)/2 by induction: adding (k + 1) to k(k + 1)/2 gives…
questions.explanation: k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, which is the formula with n = k + 1.

questions.prompt: Which is a counterexample to “if a² > b² then a > b”?
questions.explanation: 9 > 1 but −3 < 1, so the implication fails. The other pairs satisfy it.

questions.statement: A single counterexample is enough to disprove a general statement.
questions.explanation: A universal claim must hold in every case, so one failure is enough.

questions.text: To prove 6ⁿ − 1 is divisible by 5 for all n ∈ ℤ⁺, the base case gives 6¹ − 1 = ___.
questions.explanation: 5 is divisible by 5, so the statement holds for n = 1.

questions.prompt: Match each method to its description.

pairs.right: Base case, then n = k implies n = k + 1
Assume the opposite and reach an impossibility
Show one case where the claim fails
Work from known facts straight to the result

questions.explanation: Choose the method to suit the claim: induction for statements about all positive integers.

questions.prompt: In the inductive step for 6ⁿ − 1 being divisible by 5, 6ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 can be rewritten as…
questions.explanation: 6 × 6ᵏ − 1 = 6(6ᵏ − 1) + 6 − 1. Both terms are multiples of 5 by the assumption.

questions.prompt: Solve x + y + z = 6, y + z = 5, z = 3.
questions.explanation: Back-substitute: z = 3, then y = 2, then x = 6 − 5 = 1.

questions.statement: Three linear equations in three unknowns always have exactly one solution.
questions.explanation: They may have one, none or infinitely many solutions.

questions.text: If elimination produces the row 0x + 0y + 0z = 4, the system is ___.
questions.explanation: 0 = 4 is impossible, so there is no solution.

questions.prompt: Elimination on three equations leaves a row 0 = 0 and two independent equations. The system has…
options: infinitely many solutions, written with one parameter
questions.explanation: Only two independent equations constrain three unknowns, leaving one free variable.
Adding gives 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 1.

questions.text: Three planes meeting at a single point correspond to a ___ solution.
questions.explanation: The point of intersection is the only (x, y, z) satisfying all three equations.

questions.statement: If a system has infinitely many solutions, they can be written in terms of a parameter such as λ.
questions.explanation: For example x = 1 + λ, y = 2 − λ, z = λ.

questions.prompt: Match each arrangement of three planes to the solution set.

pairs.right: No solution, with no two planes parallel

questions.explanation: Algebraic outcomes correspond to geometric configurations.

questions.prompt: For which k does x + 2y = 3, 2x + 4y = k have infinitely many solutions?
questions.explanation: The second equation must be exactly double the first. For k ≠ 6 the lines are parallel and there is no solution.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of solving a 3 × 3 system by elimination.
items: Line up the equations (or write the augmented matrix)
Eliminate x from the second and third equations
Eliminate y from the third equation
Solve for z, then back-substitute for y and x
questions.explanation: Reducing to triangular form makes back-substitution straightforward.
